lead: A design is good when each module hides its own information, does one job, and leans lightly on other modules. That unpacks into a small set of design concepts: abstraction, separation of concerns, functional decomposition, modularity, information hiding, cohesion and coupling. They exist because a program too big for one head must be cut into pieces a person — and a team — can hold. Every design uses them: a payroll system that splits gross pay from deductions, a UPI app that splits the payment screen from the bank call.
prereq: You need 3.1 (the design model and quality attributes) and Unit 2 (class-based requirements models).

sections.h3: Abstraction, separation of concerns and stepwise refinement

blocks.text: An abstraction keeps what matters for the current job and drops the rest. Procedural abstraction names a sequence of steps: a call to computeGst(amount) tells you what happens, not how. Data abstraction names a set of values and the operations on them: a Bill type hides whether amounts are stored in rupees or paise.

Separation of concerns says each part of the design should deal with one concern. The tax rule, the receipt layout and the database schema are three concerns. Mixing them in one class means a change to any one disturbs the other two.

Functional decomposition is the top-down act of splitting a system into functions, then splitting each function again. Stepwise refinement applies it until every piece is small enough to write as code. A payroll system, for example, splits into three functions, and its deductions function splits once more into PF and income tax. Stop refining when the next programmer finds the step obvious.

sections.h3: Modularity, information hiding and the cost of splitting

blocks.text: A module is a named unit of software with a clear interface. Modularity is the property of a system split into such units. Good modularity makes software easier to understand, test, debug, reuse, and build in parallel.

Splitting is not free. Every interface must be designed, documented and kept stable, and every call crosses a boundary. Too many tiny modules add calls, data passing and integration work for little gain.

Information hiding says a module should hide the design decision most likely to change: a file format, a data structure, a tax rule, a device driver. Callers see only the interface. When the hidden decision changes, callers do not.
Functional decomposition and modularity are not the same thing. Decomposition is the act of splitting; modularity is the property of the result.
Two modules are functionally independent when each does one job and neither knows much about the other. Two measures describe it, and only one direction is good for each.
Cohesion looks inside a module and asks how strongly its parts belong together. Higher is better. The seven levels, worst to best, are:

head: Score
Level
What the parts share
rows: Nothing; they are bundled by accident
A similar kind; a flag picks one
They run at the same time, e.g. startup
They run in a fixed order
They work on the same data
One's output is the next one's input
All parts serve one single job

blocks.text: Coupling looks between two modules and asks how much one depends on the other. Lower is better. From worst to best:

items: Content: one module edits another's internal data or jumps into its code.
Common: both read and write the same global variable.
Control: one passes a flag that steers the other's logic.
Stamp: one passes a whole record when a single field is used.
Data: only simple data items cross the interface.

blocks.text: Worst case: two modules both increment one global counter, so a bug in either corrupts both. Best case: a caller passes one amount in rupees and receives the tax back.

Object-oriented design replaces functions with objects. A class is a template holding attributes (data) and operations (behaviour). An object is one instance of a class. Encapsulation keeps an object's data private and reachable only through its operations, which is information hiding at object level. Inheritance lets a new class reuse and extend an old one: PermanentEmployee is an Employee. Polymorphism lets one operation name behave differently per class: printPayslip() works for permanent and contract staff.

items: complete: it has every attribute and operation its responsibilities need;
sufficient: it has nothing extra, no unused field or just-in-case method;
primitive: each operation is easy to implement because it works directly on the class's own data (a method that must fetch data from five other classes is not primitive);
small and single-purpose: each operation does one thing, not five;
cohesive: all its parts serve one abstraction.

blocks.text: Refactoring is a small, behaviour-preserving change that improves structure: renaming a method, extracting a function, moving a field to the class it belongs to. It is done in tiny steps with tests run after each, so the design improves without breaking.

Aspects handle concerns that cut across many modules, such as logging or security. Instead of copying the same code into twenty classes, the concern is written once and woven in by the compiler or framework.

examples.question: One class, Billing, does four jobs: it computes GST on an amount, prints a thermal receipt, writes a row into MySQL, and sends an SMS. Use the ranking where cohesion scores 1 (coincidental, worst) to 7 (functional, best) and coupling scores 1 (content, worst) to 5 (data, best). (a) Score Billing's cohesion. (b) Split Billing into four classes plus a controller; give the class count and the cohesion score of each new class. (c) Score the coupling Billing to GstCalculator. (d) Score the coupling Billing to BillRepository when the whole Bill object is passed, and say what to pass instead.
steps: The four jobs share no data and no order. They are tied only by living in one class, so cohesion is coincidental.
Coincidental cohesion scores 1 on the 1 to 7 scale. This is the worst level.
Split into GstCalculator (tax), ReceiptPrinter (format), BillRepository (storage), SmsNotifier (message). Each now does exactly one job.
Functional cohesion scores 7 for each of the four new classes.
Billing stays as a controller that calls all four, so the class count is 4 + 1 = 5.
Billing to GstCalculator: one amount in rupees goes in, the tax amount comes back. Only simple data crosses, which is data coupling.
Data coupling scores 5 on the 1 to 5 scale. This is the best level.
Billing to BillRepository: the whole Bill object crosses while the repository needs only a few fields, which is stamp coupling.

Stamp coupling scores 4. The fix is to pass only the simple data items the repository actually uses, such as billId and amount; that reaches data coupling, score 5. A narrowed Bill DTO cuts the damage but is still a record with several fields, so it stays stamp coupling.
examples.answer: Billing's cohesion is 1 (coincidental, worst); the split gives 5 classes, each with cohesion 7 (functional); Billing to GstCalculator is data coupling, 5 (best); Billing to BillRepository is stamp coupling, 4, and passing only billId and amount gives data coupling, 5.

cohesion = {'coincidental': 1, 'logical': 2, 'temporal': 3, 'procedural': 4, 'communicational': 5, 'sequential': 6, 'functional': 7}
coupling = {'content': 1, 'common': 2, 'control': 3, 'stamp': 4, 'data': 5}
print(cohesion['coincidental'])
print(4 + 1)
print(cohesion['functional'])
print(coupling['data'])
print(coupling['stamp'])

traps: Direction slip: high cohesion is good, high coupling is bad. Writing it the other way round is the most commonly lost mark in this chapter.
Functional decomposition and modularity are different: decomposition is the act of splitting, modularity is the property of the result.
Stamp versus control coupling: passing a whole employee record for one field is stamp coupling; passing a boolean that steers the other module's logic is control coupling.
Logical cohesion groups similar functions selected by a flag, while coincidental cohesion has no relation at all. Coincidental is worse, so it scores lower, not higher.
Sequential beats communicational: parts that feed one another (output of one is input of the next) score 6; parts that merely work on the same data score 5.

quiz.q: Define cohesion and coupling in one line each, and state which direction is good for each.
quiz.a: Cohesion is how strongly the parts inside one module belong together; higher is better. Coupling is how much one module depends on another; lower is better.

quiz.q: A tax rate changes every budget. Explain how information hiding reduces the cost of that change.
quiz.a: The rate and the rule sit inside one module behind an interface such as computeTax(amount). The change is made once, inside that module, and no caller is edited or retested.

quiz.q: A class reads a CSV, validates the rows, writes two database tables inside one transaction, and mails a report built from those tables. Name its cohesion level and score it on the 1 to 7 scale.
quiz.a: The steps feed one another: the rows read are what validation checks, the validated rows are what gets written, and the report is mailed from what was written. One job's output is the next job's input, so the cohesion is sequential, score 6 (functional, 7, is better). Coincidental, score 1, would need four jobs sharing no data and no order, as in Worked example 1.

quiz.q: Module A passes a full Employee record to module B, which uses only empId. Name the coupling, score it on the 1 to 5 scale, and give the fix.
quiz.a: Stamp coupling, because a whole record crosses but one field is used. Score 4. Fix: pass only the employee id as a simple data item, giving data coupling, score 5.

quiz.q: Why can splitting a design into more and more modules lower its quality?
quiz.a: Each new module adds an interface to design, document and keep stable, plus call and data-passing overhead. Past the point where each job is already clear, extra modules raise integration effort and coupling without improving understanding.

quiz.q: A team puts logging code in thirty classes. Name the design problem and the two standard remedies.
quiz.a: Logging is a cross-cutting concern, so it is duplicated and scattered; a change to the log format touches thirty files. Remedies: an aspect woven in by the compiler or framework, or a single logger called through one interface.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry these ideas are enforced by tools, not memory: linters flag long methods and classes with too many jobs, and metrics such as LCOM estimate cohesion from the code itself. Microservice boundaries are modularity argued at the level of teams and deployment, and the same trade-off returns — more services mean more interfaces to keep stable. Search next for cohesion and coupling metrics, the single responsibility principle, and Parnas's information-hiding principle.
